newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukrainian sugar market far from sweet.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukrainian sugar market far from sweet.

text.p: Ukraine, eastern Europe's largest sugar producer, is forecasting a healthy beet harvest this year, but its sugar industry is not happy.

"The government is still using central planning methods and is anti-reform," said Vitaly Ropotilov, president of the Vinnytsia Universal Goods Exchange (Vinnytska Tovarna Universalna Birzha) in this city 300 kilometres (186 miles) east of Kiev.
"There is potential, and the harvest will be good with the rain due to stop in two to three weeks," he said from the heart of Ukraine's leading sugar-producing region.

Traditional problems in Ukraine's agricultural sector, such as the lack of money to buy fertilisers and pesticides, have been compounded in the sugar sector since Russia, a traditional buyer of Ukrainian sugar, stopped playing the nice neighbour.

Mykhailo Zubets, deputy prime minister in charge of agriculture and agriculture minister, was implementing a plan to rescue a market he described as "lost" until he was removed from his job in a cabinet reshuffle at the end of July.
The plan had producers both baffled and angry.

Ukraine has forecast a sugar beet crop of 24 to 31 million tonnes this year, against last year's 24 million tonnes, from which it produced 2.70 million tonnes of refined sugar plus 561,000 tonnes from imported raws.
Out of 1996 exports of 1.5 million tonnes, most went to Russia.
IN THE HEART OF SUGAR COUNTRY

With 39 of Ukraine's 191 sugar refineries located there, the Vinnytsia region once produced 12 percent of the Soviet Union's sugar. Six years after independence it makes just over a quarter of the sugar in a country of 50 million.
But predictions of a good crop, despite recent heavy rains, do not address problems of a cash-poor industry characterised by turn of the century refineries and machinery on its last legs.

Worse, there is no sign that Russia plans to remove a 25 percent levy imposed on top of an existing 10 percent tax in mid-May -- despite promises to do so when President Boris Yeltsin visited Ukraine later that month.
"We're at a dead end," said Ihor Rylyk, head of the National Association of Sugar Producers.

Zubets' plan, which is not expected to be changed by his removal, includes sowing less sugar beet to reduce oversupply, limiting domestic sugar sales to 1.5 million tonnes at a government-set minimum price of 1.19 hryvnias (64 cents) per kilogram (2.2 lb), and selling leftover sugar abroad at world prices.
The scheme, brainchild of the now-disbanded Ukrsukor state sugar concern, has met with criticism from producers who view it as a government grab for the market.

"These new measures stop the free sale of sugar. They are monopolistic," said Ropotilov, lobbying the government to upgrade refineries to make them more efficient and allow sugar to be traded on exchanges so a market price can be set for it.
"It's anti-reform. Reforms have to be advanced because Ukraine is poor enough."
He said the order to sell sugar for 1.19 hryvnias per kilogram, double or triple regular prices, would backfire.

"The sugar will come in from Poland and it will be sold at bazaars. No one can control it. Who will win? Poland will win," Ropotilov said. "If you sell for a specific price you must manufacture at a specific price."

The government has also promised to pay sugar beet growers 70 hryvnias per tonne, but has not yet announced where it would find the money in a country whose wage debt owed to workers reached $3.6 billion at the beginning of July.
The Ukrainian economy contracted 7.5 percent in the first six months of 1997, and 10 percent last year.
One local agricultural expert, who asked not to be named, doubted the government would pay producers.
"The government will take the sugar for itself," he said.
TRADING LEATHER FOR PARTS

About 30 minutes' drive west of Vinnytsia, along roads lined with fields of neat rows of young sugar beet, the 152-year-old Kordelivsky sugar refinery sat idle in anticipation of the harvest in September or October.
The government plans to start sugar beet testing this month.

"These refineries are monsters built in Tsarist times. They are energy-inefficient and uneconomical. When they were built nobody cared how much it cost to produce sugar," Ropotilov said, adding that rising energy costs were crippling refineries further.
Kordelivsy's director Volodymyr Mazur said the refinery has been trying to make ends meet by sewing clothes for its workers, raising cows and pigs, and making its own flour and bread.
It also engages in the common Ukrainian practice of barter, last year paying for gas with 10 percent of the 16,500 tonnes of refined sugar it produced.
"We can't wait for something to fall on our heads from the sky," Mazur said. "We have the same problems as everyone else. It's our financial state."
The refinery, a month behind in wage payments, has also in the past resorted to paying its workers with sugar.

But he was not hopeful of government plans to privatise the 191 refineries. Zubets said recently that about 70 would be privatised through Russian investors, while another ministry said 22 might be closed altogether.
"It will be a long time before we see a foreign investor," Mazur said.

One Western trader said his company, which has sharply cut the amount of sugar it trades and moved to other commodities because of too many inconsistent laws in the sector, would never consider investing in a refinery after seeing what happened to Tate and Lyle.

Local media reported the British sugar firm was pulling out of Ukraine after investing millions of dollars to start a tolling operation at a refinery in the Black Sea port city of Odessa -- because Ukraine slapped a 100 percent tax on raw sugar cane imports.
"Look at what happened to Tate and Lyle," the trader said. "This is a very, very tough market." ($ = 1.855 Ukrainian Hryvnias)
